*Main contributors: Marta Sylla, Lijing Wang, Ryan McWay*

This section outlines how we assess and value food provision as an ecosystem service within the GEP framework. The analysis focuses specifically on food provision provided by terrestrial ecosystems. This analysis does not include any aquatic ecosystem; aquaculture/fisheries is covered in a different section of the GEP manuscript. By estimating and valuing crop provision, we aim to capture the ecosystem contribution to commercial crop agricultural practices.

Crop production is defined as a contribution of the ecosystem to agricultural production of crops (United Nations et al., 2021). The contribution of the ecosystem has effective biophysical impact and consecutive economic influence. Researchers often applied these two perspectives: biophysical and economic. Biophysical perspective starts at looking at the biophysical processes or biological production functions and tries to disentangle ecosystem and human contributions. Very often the common units of energy or biomass, water inputs are used. In the economic perspective, the common monetary units are used. Crop production belongs to the provisioning group of ecosystem services (CICES Version 5.1), as well as is characterized as material contribution by the classification suggested to the concept of nature contributions to people (Brauman et al 2020).

This is a final product that enters the economy via the agricultural sector. Further modifications or processing of the initial/raw products are included in the GDP of the economic sector of Agriculture, Forestry, Fishing and Hunting, but also other sectors down the value chain. It should be noted, however, that according to the global study farmers receive, on average, 27% of the money consumers spend on food eaten at home, while they receive a significantly smaller share of the expenditure on food consumed outside home (Yi et al., 2021). This percentage varies across countries and regions, as well as changes with the quality of the raw product.

## Data and Methods

This section describes the implemented commercial crop account. The separate subsistence
calculation is not included in the formula below.

For country $c$, retained crop item $k$ and year $t$, the account calculates

$$
E_{c,k,t} = V_{c,k,t}\,r_{c,d(t)}, \qquad
E_{c,t} = \sum_{k\in K_{c,t}} E_{c,k,t}.
$$

Here $V$ is gross production value in US dollars, $r$ is the dimensionless CWoN cropland
rental share, and $d(t)$ is the most recent available decade starting no later than $t$.
$K_{c,t}$ is the set of items retained by the selection and aggregate rules below. The
base-year account uses 2019 values, expressed in 2019 USD. Summing the country values gives
the global total for that year; years are not summed together.

The rental share attributes part of crop revenue to land, following the CWoN approach.
It does not separately identify the contributions of water, soil, pollination or other
inputs. It should therefore not be interpreted as a measured share attributable to any
one of those services.

### Reported values and item selection

The calculation reads the staged FAOSTAT Value of Production bulk, retaining element 57
(gross production value in current thousand US dollars), the configured crop-item list,
and countries rather than FAOSTAT regional aggregates. The item list determines the
commercial crop scope; it is not a selection of all items in the FAOSTAT file.

FAOSTAT reports both individual items and group totals. The implemented rule drops all
configured group-total rows in a country-year when any non-group item has a nonmissing
value. It retains group totals when no individual item is valued. This is a country-year
rule, not a separate completeness check for each crop group. A retained group total cannot
be treated as an observed value for each crop within it.

### Filling missing values

At the base year, a selected country-crop pair without a reported value can take a positive
value from the staged `fao_values_1993_2024.csv` table. Existing nonmissing FAOSTAT values,
including zeros, are retained. The fill table is produced by the pollination module's FAO
preprocessing: annual production in tonnes multiplied by an annual producer price in
USD per tonne, with price fallbacks from country to subregion, region and world.

This annual-price table is distinct from the 2017–2021 median-price table used in the
pollination raster valuation. Sharing the preprocessing code does not make the two price
constructions identical. Crop provision also retains FAOSTAT's reported gross values
where they exist, rather than repricing all production with either table.

A fill requires a country code that can be linked to the rental-rate lookup. Filled rows
record the price level in `value_source`; reported values are marked `faostat`. After
filling, the code removes all price-filled rows in any country-year that still carries a
configured group-total row. This avoids adding fills alongside retained totals, but does
not establish that every removed item belongs to a particular retained group.

### Rental shares, units and outputs

The same CWoN rental share applies to reported and filled values. A missing rental share
leaves the item value missing. The calculation converts thousand USD to USD and aggregates
items to country-year totals using the account's country correspondence. Country sums
include available item values; a numeric country total does not establish complete crop
coverage.

The outputs include country-crop-year, country-year and base-year country CSVs. The country
GeoPackage attaches national values to country geometries for mapping; it is not a spatial
disaggregation within countries. A reference column carries the pre-aggregate-removal,
unfilled construction through the same rental-rate calculation for comparison. It is not
proof of the producing run behind a historical spreadsheet value.

### Relationship to the CropGrids rasters

The separate production-raster pipeline is implemented in
`../pollination/pollination_tasks.py`. It combines CropGrids harvested areas with a
Monfreda spatial yield pattern adjusted to FAO country yields, with documented fallback
rules where inputs are missing. Production is written as tonnes per square kilometre on
the CropGrids grid. Multiplying by cell area is necessary to obtain tonnes per cell.
These production rasters do not separate irrigated and rainfed production.

The pollination valuation applies prices and crop-specific pollination dependence to
production. Its pollination-value raster is therefore not a total crop-value raster or a
commercial crop-rent raster. The crop-provision task does not currently allocate its final
country-crop values to CropGrids cells.

A spatial allocation of this account would need to preserve its country totals, crop scope,
reported-value and fill rules, group-total handling and missing-value conventions.
Multiplying the existing production rasters by median prices and rental shares is a
different construction unless reconciled to those values. Such an allocation has not been
validated here.

## Validation

The implementation can be traced through `gep_calculation` in `crop_provision_tasks.py`,
`impute_missing_crop_values` and `drop_fills_under_group_totals` in
`crop_provision_functions.py`, and the selection, aggregate and rental-rate helpers in
`../utilities.py`. The annual-price construction is in `run_fao_values` and
`_merge_production_value` in `../pollination/pollination_tasks.py`.

The earlier version of this note reported a global total about 5% above CWoN. That comparison
is not established for the current selection and gap-filling rules and is not used here as
validation. Numerical reproduction of the account does not independently validate the
rental-share assumption or the completeness of every country's crop coverage.

## Coverage

The published table is one row for each of the account's 250 countries, base year 2019, in constant 2019 USD. Of the 250, 174 carry a value, 24 are computed zeros, and 52 rows are missing, kept as missing rather than zero because an input carries no data for those countries. A zero means the computation returned zero; a missing row means the data to compute one is absent.
